3.text: gather for a performance, if possible for a contest of ability and inspiration.

4.text: The principal heir¹ makes a circle around the hearth, hopping in a

5.text: curious way, and keeping his heels close together. The master of the house,

6.text: who sits on a skin near the sleeping-room, begins to shout, repeating many

7.text: times the same loud double cry, “Yoho, yoho!” One by one the people join

8.text: him; others start singing, and the tent fairly vibrates with the deafening noise.

9.text: There are no rules about the singing. Each sings his own particular tune,

10.text: and stops for a rest when he feels tired. Those who have drums beat them

11.text: for a while and pass them to the others. The drums for the ceremony are

12.text: gathered from the whole camp, and sometimes as many as ten may be used

13.text: in the performance. After a while the dance begins. One name for it is

14.text: “the shaking-off thin” (têwlaˊɪrg̣ɪn), and it purports to shake off diseases and

15.text: evil spirits from the body of the performer.

16.text: The dancers are formed into two-sets, placed on opposite sides of the

17.text: hearth. One set stand on the outer side of the hearth, with their backs

18.text: toward the entrance: they are chiefly elderly men. The other set stand on

19.text: the inner side of the hearth. They have their backs turned toward the

20.text: sleeping-room, and face their partners at the entrance. These are women,

21.text: who put on their overcoats, adorned with fringe and pendants. The first set

22.text: are considered the more important; they are called “ceremonial movers”

23.text: (mñiničuˊlɪt). The second set are termed “the standing ones” (vêʟaˊlɪt), or

24.text: “the standing women” (vêˊʟa-ñeˊus˙qatti), meaning that they are standing on

25.text: their feet while the onlookers remain seated.

26.text: The dance is usually opened by the master and the mistress of the house,

27.text: while the others sit in their places. On this occasion the master of the house

28.text: is called “road-maker,” because he opens the road for the others. A skin is

29.text: spread on the ground under his feet. He beats his family drum, using, in-

30.text: stead of the whalebone, the wooden drum-stick, with which he strikes the

31.text: wooden rim of the drum from underneath. He and the woman sing different

32.text: tunes, each choosing what he or she likes. He usually starts with the here-

33.text: ditary tunes of his family, then he passes to those that he himself has com-

34.text: posed at various times. Each tune is repeated again and again for several

35.text: minutes. The woman sings those which she has learned from her mother, or

36.text: has composed by herself for her own amusement. Husband and wife each

37.text: perform a dance, in which their motions are more or less alike. They keep

38.text: the same place, swaying their bodies and swinging their hands, now to the

39.text: right, then to the left. From time to time they squat down and immediately

40.text: jump up again. At length the first performers give up their places to others,

41.text: who at first appear singly, taking turns one by one. After a while, several
